newsitem.title: USA: Tough guy film, TV actor Robert Mitchum dies.
newsitem.headline: Tough guy film, TV actor Robert Mitchum dies.

text.p: Actor Robert Mitchum, the sleepy-eyed, barrel-chested star of more than 125 films, died in his sleep early on Tuesday. He was 79.

Mitchum, who starred in such films as "Cape Fear" and "Night of the Hunter" as well as the epic TV miniseries "The Winds of War" and "War and Remembrance," died at his home in Santa Barbara around 5 a.m. PDT (1200 GMT), according to his agent, Jack Gilardi.
Mitchum had been suffering from emphysema for more than a year and was diagnosed with lung cancer last spring.
"We've not only lost a great man and a great actor but we've also lost a great friend," Gilardi said.

Mitchum had a distinctive baritone voice that allowed him to be vaguely threatening in heroic roles and oddly sympathetic as a villain. He also had an image in Hollywood as a "bad boy" that was fuelled by a 1948 arrest for marijuana possession, which led to six months in a work camp.

The notoriety inspired a new popularity. He went on to star in, among other things, "Ryan's Daughter" (1970), "The Friends of Eddie Coyle" (1973), "The Big Sleep" (1978) and, in 1983, the ABC television miniseries "The Winds of War," which brought him some of his greatest attention later in his career.

His workmanlike approach to his craft grew from an unstable past. Born on Aug. 6, 1917, in Bridgeport, Connecticut, he was soon left fatherless and led a gypsy-like childhood, frequently moving, always struggling.
As a young man in the 1930s, he wandered the country and the world, working as an engine wiper on a freighter, a nightclub bouncer, a boxer, a ditchdigger and a publicist for an astrologer.
In 1940, he married his high school sweetheart, Dorothy Spence, and settled down to raising a family and working for a California aircraft company.

Unhappy there, he signed on as an extra in "pictures," as he always called movies. Appearances in Westerns led to bit parts in a string of "B" movies and two big war films, "Cry Havoc" and "Gung Ho!," both released in 1943.

In 1944 he won praise for a mystery thriller, "When Strangers Marry," with Kim Novak, and another war film, "Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo," whose director Mervyn LeRoy told him: "You're either the lousiest actor in the world or the best."
In 1945, Mitchum made the big time as the rugged but weary captain of "The Story of GI Joe," based on the war memoirs of war correspondent Ernie Pyle.
The role earned Mitchum an Academy Award nomination for best supporting actor, but he did not show up at the ceremony.
Soon he was drafted into the Army and served as a private.

His return to Hollywood brought renewed success with Jane Greer in "Out of the Past" (1947), a private-eye thriller, and with Loretta Young in "Rachel and the Stranger" (1948) in which Mitchum went against type and sang.
In 1948, he also starred in one of his best Westerns, playing a heroic stranger in "Blood on the Moon."

That year also witnessed his marijuana arrest which threatened his career, but he treated it with typical tough guy aplomb. Asked what the work camp was like, he replied: "Just like Palm Springs. Without the riff-raff, of course."

In 1949, he appeared in "The Red Pony," but a string of forgettable movies followed. In 1954, Mitchum played Marilyn Monroe's laconic escort in the hit "River of No Return" and also scored big as a selfish doctor in "Not As a Stranger." Another of his best roles, and one of his most complex, came a year later, with "The Night of the Hunter," an acclaimed but less financially successful film in which he played a murderous preacher.
Hits and misses followed through the 1960s. Successes included "Heaven Knows, Mr. Allison" (1957), "Home From the Hill" (1960), "The Sundowners" (1960), "Cape Fear" (1962) and "El Dorado" (1967).

In the 1970s, Mitchum turned aside thoughts of retiring. He starred as a remorseful wife-murderer in "Going Home" (1971), a defrocked priest in "The Wrath of God" (1972) and a tired crook in "The Friends of Eddie Coyle" (1975).
In 1975, Mitchum was brilliantly cast as the laconic detective Philip Marlowe in a remake of Raymond Chandler's "Farewell My Lovely," a role he repeated in 1978 in "The Big Sleep."

In 1980, Mitchum reversed his stand against television and agreed to do a TV movie, the 16-hour miniseries "The Winds of War." As Navy Capt. Pug Henry, his stern but human presence gave a solid centre to a show otherwise steeped in soap opera.
In 1991 he appeared in a remake of "Cape Fear" with Robert De Niro and Nick Nolte.

Despite brief separations in 1948 and 1953, Mitchum remained married to his wife Dorothy. Of their three children, two, James and Christopher, have occasionally worked as actors and the third, Petrine, worked for a movie production company.
